indicators.label: Growing degree days (May–Sep)

indicators.label: Longest summer dry spell (Jun–Aug)
indicators.description: Longest run of days with less than 0.04 in (1 mm) of rain.

indicators.label: Average summer high (Jun–Aug)

indicators.label: Crop water demand (May–Sep)
indicators.description: Evapotranspiration: the water a well-watered crop would use and the air would take, May to September. Worked out from daily temperatures with the FAO Hargreaves method. Hotter seasons raise it.
indicators.source: Average of NASA POWER (50 km) and NASA Daymet (1 km) daily rain and temperature, 1991–2025; root-zone soil wetness from NASA POWER

indicators.label: Water balance: rain minus demand (May–Sep)
indicators.description: Growing-season rain minus crop water demand. The more negative it is, the more a crop depends on water stored in the soil or on irrigation.
indicators.source: Average of NASA POWER (50 km) and NASA Daymet (1 km) daily rain and temperature, 1991–2025; root-zone soil wetness from NASA POWER

indicators.label: Root-zone soil wetness (Jun–Aug)
indicators.description: How full of water the soil is where roots grow, June to August (0% = dry, 100% = saturated). From NASA's MERRA-2 land model via NASA POWER: a satellite-era model estimate for a 30-mile grid square, not a probe in your field.

facts.text: A fallow season (no crop, weeds controlled) stores roughly a quarter of the rain that falls during it in the soil, which raises the next crop's yield in dry areas, at the cost of a year without income and more erosion risk on bare ground.
facts.source: Great Plains dryland research, e.g. K-State and USDA-ARS Akron (approximate)

facts.text: Adding a small grain (wheat or oats) breaks corn and soybean pest cycles and opens a summer window for a legume cover crop.
Compared with continuing the current pattern (Corn → Winter wheat → Corn): estimated +$2/acre per year, 34 lb/acre less nitrogen over 3 years, and a soil-health score of 36 vs 48 out of 100.

facts.text: Ask your agronomist about: Confirm local planting, harvest and stress windows for each crop; these are model reference calendars, not observed field phenology. Replace approximate yield potentials, prices and input costs with local budgets; modeled yields and profit are not research-plot observations or field guarantees. Check stored soil water and whether rain-only production is viable for these phases. Confirm the winter-wheat sowing window after the preceding harvest and local winter survival. Review fallow weed control, residue retention and erosion risk; no crop does not mean observed bare soil.
No corn-rootworm benefit is assigned to this plan without corn; benefits for other pests are undocumented here.

explanation.summary: NASA data for your field near Finney County, KS shows growing degree days (May–Sep) rising by about 68 °F·days per decade, and that change is statistically real. Recommended for a balance of profit, soil and risk: Fallow (no crop) → Winter wheat → Grain sorghum. Compared with continuing the current pattern (Corn → Winter wheat → Corn): estimated +$2/acre per year, 34 lb/acre less nitrogen over 3 years, and a soil-health score of 36 vs 48 out of 100.
explanation.speech: NASA data for your field near Finney County, KS shows growing degree days rising by about 68 degree days per decade, and that change is statistically real. Focusing on a balance of profit, soil and risk, I suggest fallow in 2027, then winter wheat in 2028, then grain sorghum in 2029. It needs about 34 pounds per acre less nitrogen over three years than your current pattern. Please check with your county extension agent before buying seed.
explanation.sms: SoilSense plan: 2027 Fallow (no crop); 2028 Winter wheat; 2029 Grain sorghum. Based on NASA climate data 1991-2025. Check with your extension agent.

assumptions: Heat stress uses extreme-heat degree days above each crop's threshold (the measure used in Schlenker & Roberts, PNAS 2009); irrigation is assumed to remove about two-thirds of heat damage.
Climate history is shifted to today's conditions only where a trend is statistically significant (Mann-Kendall, p < 0.05).
Years from the last decade count twice when scoring climate fit.
A crop-year counts as stressed when its combined water, heat, season-length and planting-condition score falls below 0.6.

Each 3-year plan is replayed against every run of consecutive NASA weather years, carrying soil water from one season to the next: crops draw stored water down, and between crops the soil stores about 50% of cool-season (Nov–Mar) rain and 15% of warm-season rain. A winter cover crop uses about 40% of that recharge.
Effective in-season rainfall = 75% of season rain; the soil can hold 80% of its available water capacity, to 2 m or the depth of the soil.

Yield = water-unlimited potential × the share of the crop's water need that was met (a water-production function, with no grain below a crop-specific minimum) × heat, season-length and planting stress.
Yield potential: dry Plains states use approximate irrigated-practice yields; other states use state (or USDA NASS county) averages × 1.1, since average farm yields reach about 85–90% of potential.
Nitrogen, seed and other input costs scale with the expected yield (yield-goal method), so low-yield rain-fed crops are budgeted more cheaply.
Fallow (a season with no crop, only weed control at about $45/acre) is offered only on rain-fed fields with under about 25 inches of rain a year.
Irrigated fields: water need is met and about $110/acre pumping cost is added.
Prices, costs, yield potentials and rotation yield effects are approximate defaults in src/engine/crops.ts and src/engine/regions.ts; replace them with local budgets.
Winter wheat cannot be sown for the first plan year once its fall planting window has passed.
Water: rain only. Pumping costs about $8 per inch of water per acre.
Bad years out of 10: how often a crop would have been badly stressed when replayed through the 35 years of NASA weather (shifted to today's climate trends), averaged over the plan's crops.
Yield potential is calibrated to real USDA NASS harvests for rain-fed fields: recent average ÷ the share of potential the model says recent weather allowed (kept within 60–115% of the state value).
Corn yield basis: USDA Southwest district average for rain-fed fields, 3 reports up to 2018.
Soybean yield basis: county average for 2 recent years × 51% (how rain-fed fields compared with all fields in 7 years of county records).
Winter wheat yield basis: USDA Southwest district average for rain-fed fields, 4 reports up to 2019.
Grain sorghum yield basis: county average for 2 recent years × 83% (how rain-fed fields compared with all fields in 17 years of county records).

Prices: USDA NASS prices received, average of the latest months — corn $4.19/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), soybean $10.88/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), winter wheat $5.38/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), oats $3.14/bu (national, 12 months to Sep 2026), alfalfa (hay) $123.83/ton (state, 12 months to Sep 2026), grain sorghum $3.62/bu (state, 12 months to Sep 2026). Other prices are defaults.
This area averages about 21 inches of rain a year; fallow was considered.

Replayed past years are history, not a forecast: each uses that year's real NASA weather on this soil, compared with what the county really harvested (USDA NASS) and why crop insurance paid out (USDA RMA).
